meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
Hale. My son found out about a zero on his phone, in class. On what basis?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.
Pretty conclusive. The company that makes it says its indicator should not be the sole basis for action against a student, and I have that printed in my bag. What else do you have?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. Go on.

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.
I'm writing those times down. A boy who drafts somewhere else and pastes it in looks exactly like that. Did you ask him before you entered the zero?

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
It's not there. A seventeen-year-old getting a quotation wrong is a bad citation, not proof of where it came from. And you skipped my question: was he heard before the mark went in?
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
Students change their argument between an outline and an essay; that's what an outline is for. I've asked twice whether he was heard first. I'm taking your silence as a no.

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.

Fine, you asked him first. Forty minutes in class in September is not the same test as an essay written at home, and five minutes after class with a nervous seventeen-year-old is your notes, not his words. What is it you want to happen now, Hale?

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.
He'll do it, to put this behind him and for no other reason. Private, nothing on file, and I'll want that email tonight. When does he sit it, because his applications close December 1?
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Okay. Thursday, November 12, after school. Put that date in tonight's email, and the zero comes out of the gradebook when his mark goes in.
Do we have an agreement?
Yes, once it's in my inbox tonight. I have ten minutes.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL

cc: Principal, Elbow Crossing High School

Hale,

In our meeting today you agreed that Owen will sit a private, supervised rewrite under procedure 4.4 on Thursday, November 12, after school, that its mark will replace the zero, and that nothing will go on his record. I still require that agreement in writing, with the date in it, and the zero removed from the gradebook when his new mark is entered. You said I would have it in writing tonight and the mark entered well before December 1.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF

Where she ended: last position. She agreed to a private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12, after school, with its mark replacing the zero and nothing on his record, and she still wants that in writing tonight and the zero taken out of the gradebook when the new mark goes in. That is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4, and you reached it before her time ran out.

What moved her: you answered her question about whether Owen was heard first, with your dated notes from November 2, the day before the zero went in. Procedure and dated paper are what she trusts, and after that she stopped attacking and asked what you wanted.

What cost ground: you opened with the checker score of 94 percent and called it pretty conclusive. To her that is a machine's opinion, and it handed her the attack she came prepared to make.

What she never said: in October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked. Your version history came very close to that night, with the essay arriving in two large edits at 11:52 PM and 11:58 PM on Wednesday, October 28, and she wrote the times down and went straight to procedure. It proves nothing about the essay; it is why she fought so hard.

Try next time: when she first asked whether you spoke to Owen before entering the zero, answer it right then with your November 2 notes instead of moving on to the next document and making her ask twice.
